The proposal has not selected either definition, so ‘inside the kernel’ should not be equated with ‘incapable of failure.’
Why use a confidence set as well as a belief? Aren’t they both just uncertainty?

They track different uncertainty. The belief concerns the hidden state given the learner’s observations; the confidence set concerns which environment or reward-and-hazard models remain plausible. A safety judgment could fail if it accounts for one but treats the other as known. A proposed kernel would have to say how it handles their interaction at each decision.
Could I certify an action because it looks safe under one model in the confidence set?

That would not be enough. If another still-plausible model makes the action dangerously likely to cause an irreversible failure, favorable risk under the first model does not justify taking it. Certification needs a risk claim that remains valid across the uncertainty relevant at the time of action, or a justified probabilistic treatment of that uncertainty whose errors are counted toward the overall safety guarantee.
Does building a belief safety kernel give us a known safe exploration policy after all?

Not merely by proposing to build one. A kernel would be an inferred, history-dependent way to assess permissible decisions, not necessarily an exploration policy supplied in advance. But the construction must confront the first decision: it cannot assume that an unknown kernel has already been found or that the learner can safely take uncertified actions while discovering it. The assumptions need to make an initial pre-action safety assessment possible without stipulating a complete safe exploration policy.
What if the confidence set initially contains models with conflicting views of every informative action?

Then the proposed kernel might certify no distinguishing probe. Unless other safe observations can narrow the confidence set, reward-model elimination may stall. A sufficient-condition argument would need to establish access to useful, certifiable information from the learner’s actual initial uncertainty; it cannot infer that access merely from the fact that a rewarding policy exists in each model.
What is a certified distinguishing probe in this setup?

It is an interaction that the kernel can justify **before it is taken** and whose observations help distinguish reward models that remain plausible. Both parts matter: a probe can be informative but unjustifiably risky, or certifiably safe but irrelevant to choosing rewarding actions. The proposal depends on probes that are both usable under the risk limit and informative about decisions that matter to the constrained informed-policy comparison.
Would any observation that differs across two reward models count as distinguishing?

It could be evidence of distinguishability, but the difference needs to be useful at a feasible cost. If the observation laws differ so little that many low-reward probes are needed, eliminating a model might take too long for Õ(√T) regret. The analysis would need a quantitative link between the information a certified probe supplies and the reward lost before the learner can make competitive choices.
Why eliminate reward models instead of simply estimating the best reward?

Elimination gives one possible decision structure: maintain plausible reward models, take certified probes that discriminate among models whose recommended actions differ, and remove a model only when observations justify doing so. It can make the information goal explicit. But it is a proposed mechanism, not a requirement that every successful learner eliminate models, and erroneous elimination of the true model would need to be controlled.
Could the confidence set used for safety and the set of reward models being eliminated be the same object?

They might overlap or be represented together, but the proposal does not fix that architecture. The important requirements are that uncertainty relevant to irreversible hazards stays in the safety assessment and that reward-model elimination uses valid evidence from certified interactions. Learning something about rewards should not silently remove a hazard possibility unless the observations also justify that safety inference.
Do we need the probe to distinguish every reward model from every other one?

Not necessarily. For regret, it may be enough to distinguish models that would lead the optimal informed, safety-constrained policy to make materially different reward decisions. Models that prescribe equivalent behavior for that comparison need not be separated for their own sake. The proposed elimination rule would still need to define what counts as a material decision difference and bound the loss caused by remaining ambiguity.
What if two reward models recommend different actions, but the kernel allows neither probe that would distinguish them?

That exposes a possible obstruction. The learner might have to choose without the information the informed comparator possesses, or refrain from an advantageous action indefinitely. To support Õ(√T) regret, the assumptions must ensure a certified route to resolving consequential ambiguity, or show that unresolved ambiguity has only a sufficiently small regret cost. The existence of a distinguishing probe outside the kernel would not close the gap.
Does the kernel need to include the informed policy’s actions from the beginning?

Not necessarily from the beginning. Temporary restrictions can reflect genuine model uncertainty. But if the kernel permanently excludes actions needed to approach the optimal informed policy satisfying the same safety constraint, the reward gap may persist. A regret analysis must account quantitatively for the time spent probing and for any delay in certifying competitive actions.
Could an action be safe for the informed policy but uncertifiable for the learner?

Yes. The informed policy knows the environment, while the learner’s confidence set may contain other possibilities. A sound learner may therefore decline an action the informed policy could safely take. This proposal has to show that certified distinguishing probes resolve such uncertainty quickly enough for the learner’s additional reward loss to meet the Õ(√T) target.
How do we translate kernel membership into the 1% statement?

The construction must justify the conditional failure risk of decisions actually made and combine those risks across the learner’s adaptive history. It must also account for the chance that the confidence set, belief assessment, or certificate is wrong in a way that leads to failure. The final claim is a single bound: the probability of **at least one irreversible failure during learning** is at most **1%**. Kernel membership alone, without that whole-run argument, is insufficient.
So giving every kernel-approved probe a risk below 1% would not be enough?

Correct. Multiple probes can accumulate risk. The 1% is a cumulative limit, not a separate allowance per probe or time step. A kernel-based decision rule would need to keep track of how much justified risk remains as it probes and later exploits, with a guarantee that its adaptive choices collectively respect that limit.
Would an inaccurate belief be covered by the confidence set?

Not automatically. A confidence set over possible models does not, by itself, guarantee that the learner’s belief about hidden states is accurate at the decision point. The proposal needs a justified relationship between its filtering procedure, the confidence set, and the action-risk bounds the kernel uses. A certificate based on a belief that understates a hazard could be false even if the true environment model has not been excluded.
Does the kernel have to be invariant forever once we enter it?

That depends on its formal definition. A conventional safety-kernel idea suggests maintaining a region in which future decisions can continue to satisfy the safety requirement, but the proposal does not prescribe an invariant or zero-risk region. If the kernel is used for a finite-horizon risk budget, its membership may depend on the belief, confidence set, remaining allowance, and time. Whatever definition is chosen must support the actual whole-learning-period guarantee rather than relying on the name ‘kernel.’
What if we use observations from certified probes to shrink both uncertainty sets?

That is consistent with the proposal if the observations justify both updates. A probe outcome may eliminate reward models and could also refine a belief or a safety-relevant model confidence set. The proof must keep the validity of those updates separate: evidence that distinguishes rewards need not distinguish hazards, and removing an unsafe possibility without sufficient evidence could invalidate later certificates.
Should elimination be aggressive to get the Õ(√T) rate?

It has to be efficient, but aggressive elimination without valid evidence can exclude the true reward model and create persistent regret. A rate proof would need to balance how quickly certified observations narrow the models against the probability and cost of an incorrect elimination. The proposal specifies the desired Õ(√T) regret rate, not an elimination threshold or update rule.
What precisely is the oracle for the regret calculation?

It is the **optimal informed policy satisfying the same safety constraint**. It knows the relevant environment for the comparison, but it does not have permission to disregard the 1% limit on irreversible failure. Regret measures the learner’s cumulative reward shortfall over horizon T relative to that constrained policy; the exact reward treatment of failure would need to be specified in a formal result.
Why target Õ(√T) rather than just any sublinear rate?

It is the quantitative target of this proposal. Õ(√T) would imply sublinear growth in T, up to the factors suppressed by the notation, if proved under clearly stated parameter dependencies. A proof must account for the cost of certified probing, incorrect or unresolved reward-model decisions, safety-induced restrictions, and any failure-related reward loss. Simply showing eventual model elimination would not establish that rate.
Could a 1% failure bound create linear expected regret even if model elimination is fast?

Potentially. If an irreversible failure prevents reward collection for much of horizon T, a probability that remains near 1% can contribute order-T expected loss. The expected-regret argument would need to control that contribution, possibly with a tighter horizon-dependent failure bound while still meeting the 1% ceiling, or with a clearly specified regret formulation that handles failures differently. The safety ceiling alone cannot prove Õ(√T) regret.
What would the explicit, nontrivial assumptions need to cover?

They would need to make the belief and model-confidence assessments reliable before consequential actions, ensure the safety kernel initially permits some justified way to gather information, and provide certified probes that quantitatively distinguish reward models with different constrained-oracle choices. They would also need to support whole-run risk accounting and efficient reward-model elimination. Merely assuming ‘the kernel is safe’ and ‘the probes reveal rewards’ would restate the desired conclusions rather than explain when they follow.
Could we claim this is a characterization of when safe reward discovery is possible?

Not from the proposal alone. A proved result under explicit assumptions could provide a sufficient route: build a confidence-set belief safety kernel, use certified distinguishing probes to eliminate consequential reward ambiguity, and bound risk and regret. Calling it a full characterization would require a justified account of cases outside those assumptions as well. The proposal does not establish necessity.
Can you condense the approach without making it sound completed?

**Proposal:** Construct **confidence-set belief safety kernels** that certify probes before they are taken. Use those probes to eliminate reward models that imply different constrained-oracle choices, while accounting for their cumulative risk so the probability of **any irreversible failure during learning is at most 1%**. Aim to bound the resulting regret by **Õ(√T)** against the optimal informed policy under the same safety constraint. Kernel validity, access to distinguishing probes, whole-run safety, and the regret rate remain to be proved.
Can data-derived belief safety kernels include the constrained oracle’s informative actions before any irreversible trial without assuming a safe baseline?

That is the central question for a kernel-based approach. A possible answer depends on what information the learner has *before* its first irreversible trial. The data would need to justify safety assessments despite uncertainty about both the hidden state and the environment, while the resulting kernel would need to admit actions informative enough to approach the optimal informed policy under the same safety constraint. Neither property follows simply from constructing a kernel or from knowing that the informed policy has informative actions.
What would it mean for the kernel to include an informative action before the learner knows the true model?

At the decision point, the learner’s current belief and set of plausible models would have to support approving that action without assuming which model is true. Its potential to reveal reward information is separate from the justification for taking it. An action the informed policy can safely choose in the true model may not be certifiable while the learner still considers another model in which it is hazardous.
Is requiring the kernel to include every action the oracle might take too demanding?

Possibly. The regret objective does not necessarily require immediate approval of every oracle action. It requires a feasible route through certified interactions to learning and eventually using the choices needed to compete with the optimal informed, safety-constrained policy, at sublinear cumulative cost. But if every route to the necessary information remains excluded, merely allowing other safe actions will not solve the reward-discovery problem.
When I say ‘before any irreversible trial,’ am I requiring the kernel to know the outcome of that trial?

No; it is the opposite. Inclusion must be justified from data and observations available *without first conducting* an irreversible trial. Outcomes of later probes may refine the kernel for subsequent choices, but cannot retroactively certify the first probe. This timing prevents a circular argument in which taking a dangerous action is treated as the way to discover whether it was safe to take.
What data could make such an initial judgment possible without a baseline policy?

Conceptually, data available before the consequential choice could provide safety-relevant information about the proposed action and the learner’s present circumstances. The question does not specify a data source or guarantee its adequacy. A formal condition would have to state what the learner receives initially, how that information bears on hidden-state hazards, and why its uncertainty bounds are valid for the actions the kernel admits. Such information is different from supplying a policy that already tells the learner how to explore safely.
Does ‘data-derived’ mean we can ignore how those data were collected?

No. Their provenance matters for interpreting a safety certificate and the scope of any failure guarantee. If gathering the data is part of the learning period, irreversible risks taken during collection belong in the bound on the probability of any failure during learning. If the data are supplied beforehand, a target-learning guarantee does not by itself certify the safety of their prior collection. Either way, the data must actually support the kernel’s pre-action risk assessments.
Could the data describe an action under other beliefs without supporting it under the learner’s current belief?

Yes. A belief safety kernel is sensitive to uncertainty about the hidden state at the moment of action. Evidence about an action in circumstances represented by one belief need not bound its risk under a different belief. To include an oracle-relevant informative action, the derivation must connect the available data to the learner’s *current* pre-action information, rather than transfer a safety label without justification.
Would a sufficiently conservative kernel be safe even if it excludes all informative actions?

It might restrict irreversible risk, but that would leave the reward-learning requirement unanswered. The question asks for a kernel that includes the informative actions needed for the constrained-oracle comparison, not just one that declines every consequential probe. Safety and useful coverage have to be examined together.
How could the learner certify an action when its confidence set contains a hazardous alternative?

It would need some justified way to resolve or bound that alternative before acting. If available observations narrow the confidence set safely, the action might become certifiable afterward. If the alternative remains plausible and assigns too much irreversible-failure risk to the action, approving it based solely on the favorable model would not be a valid certificate. The question is whether data-derived updates offer a path to inclusion without relying on an irreversible diagnostic trial.
Does the oracle itself need the kernel to include those actions?

The informed oracle is the comparison policy, not a learner constrained by the learner’s uncertainty-based kernel. It must satisfy the *same safety constraint*, but it can condition on its knowledge of the environment. The kernel’s coverage question is whether the learner can access the relevant informative and eventual reward choices while preserving that shared constraint; equality between the learner’s initial admissible set and the oracle’s action set is not presumed.
Would inclusion require proof of zero failure risk?

Not necessarily. The safety target is a probability of **any irreversible failure during learning of at most 1%**, so an action with justified nonzero risk could be approved if its use fits a valid whole-period risk argument. A kernel definition could be stricter, but its name alone does not imply zero risk. Nor does a risk estimate for one action automatically justify repeated uses within the 1% limit.
What would make including an action impossible to justify from the available data?

A key obstruction is indistinguishability: two plausible hidden-state or environment possibilities could agree on everything the learner has observed before the trial, while assigning incompatible hazards to that same informative action. If no alternative pre-action information separates or conservatively bounds them, the learner cannot simply certify the favorable case. Whether that obstruction applies to a particular proposed kernel would need to be demonstrated, not assumed.
If the kernel includes an oracle action but not a probe that tells us when to take it, is that enough?

No. Inclusion of an eventual action does not supply the information needed to choose it in the right target circumstances. The learner needs certified access to *distinguishing* interactions, or other justified observations, that resolve reward-relevant uncertainty. Conversely, certified diagnostic probes without access to the actions their observations recommend may also leave a persistent gap against the informed policy.
Could the kernel expand as observations arrive without starting from a known safe baseline?

In principle, yes, if the learner can obtain the initial observations and make any intervening decisions within the safety requirement. Expansion must follow valid updates to its belief and model uncertainty; it cannot be assumed to happen after an uncertified action. The hard part is establishing a safe and informative starting point without sneaking a complete safe exploration policy into the assumptions.
Does an initial safe starting point amount to a safe baseline after all?

Not automatically. A condition that certain information is available before acting, or that a particular initial decision can be assessed from that information, is not the same as giving the learner a known policy for safely exploring throughout the task. But if the assumption effectively supplies a fully specified sequence of informative safe actions, the distinction would lose substance. A formal claim should say exactly what is initially known and what the learner still has to infer.
How do I test whether the kernel really covers the oracle’s informative actions?

Specify the oracle-relevant reward distinctions and the actions or observations that would resolve them. Then, from each belief and confidence set the learner could reach before resolving those distinctions, check whether a feasible sequence of data-certified decisions supplies the needed information. Assess both when those actions become admissible and the reward cost of waiting; eventual coverage alone need not support sublinear constrained-oracle regret.
Would the kernel have to admit an informative action in every possible belief?

That depends on the scope of the desired guarantee. It need not admit the same probe everywhere, or probe when all plausible models already recommend equivalent constrained-oracle behavior. But for beliefs at which consequential ambiguity persists, a sufficient result needs an accessible way to reduce it, or an argument that the unresolved ambiguity costs only sublinear regret. Such a condition has to concern beliefs the learning procedure may actually encounter, including its initial one.
What role does model elimination play in checking that access?

Certified distinguishing observations could justify removing reward models from the learner’s plausible set, potentially allowing further actions to enter the kernel. The test must ensure that elimination uses evidence the learner could safely acquire and does not mistakenly remove a hazard-relevant possibility without justification. It must also bound how long consequential reward ambiguity persists, rather than treating the possibility of eventual elimination as enough.
If the data give a valid safety certificate but no reward information, what have we answered?

Only the safety part for the actions covered by that certificate. The question specifically asks whether the kernel includes the constrained oracle’s *informative* actions before irreversible trials. A certificate that permits only uninformative behavior could still leave the learner unable to discover rewards at acceptable regret cost. Coverage must refer to decision-relevant information, not just a nonempty kernel.
Can I infer a 1% guarantee from kernel membership alone?

No. The safety argument must cover the learner’s full adaptive sequence and any errors in the data-derived belief or confidence set. The target is that the probability of **at least one irreversible failure during learning** is at most **1% overall**, not that each admitted action individually has risk below 1%. Kernel membership is meaningful only through a defined certificate and cumulative risk argument.
And can I infer Õ(√T) regret from coverage alone?

No. Even when informative actions are admissible, the learner may require too many costly probes or wait too long before they become available. An Õ(√T) claim needs quantitative bounds on information gained, reward forgone, any persistent kernel restrictions, and failure-related loss under the chosen regret definition, all relative to the optimal informed policy satisfying the same safety constraint.
How would you state the unresolved issue compactly?

Can initial data and subsequent safely obtained observations support **valid pre-action belief-kernel certificates** for a sequence of probes that distinguishes consequential reward models, without assuming a known safe exploration policy or first taking an irreversible trial? To answer yes in a specified class of POMDPs, one would still have to show that this sequence retains access to the constrained oracle’s relevant choices, bounds the probability of **any irreversible failure during learning by 1%**, and permits the proposed low-regret comparison. The question itself does not establish those conditions.

Here is a hypothesis for the initial-kernel question: if passive cues bound transition uncertainty below γ/2 and the constrained oracle’s informative probes have γ viability margins, then confidence-set belief safety kernels include those probes initially. Does that make sense?

Yes, as a conditional hypothesis. The proposed logic is that passive cues constrain uncertainty about transitions *before* an irreversible trial, while each oracle probe has a viability margin large enough to tolerate that uncertainty. If the confidence-set kernel evaluates viability robustly over the models and beliefs the learner still considers possible, those bounds might let it include the probes from the start. The key implication—uncertainty below γ/2 plus a γ margin yields initial inclusion—still needs a precise definition and proof.
Why specify initial inclusion rather than eventual inclusion?

Initial inclusion addresses whether the learner can take an informative action without first conducting an irreversible trial or relying on a known safe exploration policy. Eventual inclusion could depend on information obtained through a probe the learner could not initially justify. The hypothesis proposes to break that potential circle by making passive pre-action information sufficient for an initial kernel assessment.
What does it mean for passive cues to bound transition uncertainty?

They would have to constrain the possible transitions relevant to the proposed probes, using information available before those probes are taken. A formal statement must define the uncertainty measure and show that the bound is valid for the learner’s initial information. Merely observing a cue, or having a bound for unrelated transitions, would not justify including an oracle probe in the kernel.
Is ‘below γ/2’ a claim about the probability of irreversible failure?

No. It is the hypothesized bound on **transition uncertainty**. The γ viability margin describes a separate safety-relevant gap. Neither number is itself a failure probability. To use the inequality, the analysis has to connect transition uncertainty to how much the kernel’s viability assessment could change.
Can I simply subtract γ/2 from the γ viability margin and declare the probe safe?

Only if the quantities are defined in compatible terms and a justified bound says that the stipulated transition uncertainty can erode the viability margin by no more than the amount being subtracted. That translation is not supplied by the hypothesis. The appealing arithmetic suggests a possible proof strategy, but it cannot substitute for showing how transition uncertainty affects the actual belief-kernel decision.
Would the strict word ‘below’ matter?

Yes. The stated premise is transition uncertainty **below γ/2**, not merely an unspecified small amount or a bound at some unrelated scale. A formal result should preserve that strict inequality and define where it holds. It should also explain whether a bound close to γ/2 still leaves enough margin under the kernel’s particular viability test.
What is a γ viability margin meant to protect?

It is meant to provide slack between an oracle probe’s viability assessment and the boundary at which the confidence-set kernel would reject it. The formal definition must identify that boundary, the belief and plausible models involved, and how a transition perturbation affects the assessment. Calling a probe ‘γ-viable’ without specifying those elements would not establish that an uncertain learner can certify it.
Whose view of the probe supplies the margin: the informed oracle’s or the learner’s?

That distinction must be resolved in the hypothesis’s formalization. A margin known only under the true model may not survive the other models in the learner’s initial confidence set. For **initial inclusion** in a confidence-set kernel, the argument must connect the oracle probe’s γ margin to the robust assessment the learner can make from its own initial belief and data. It cannot silently give the learner the oracle’s knowledge.
Could an oracle probe have a γ margin in the true environment but be excluded by the learner’s confidence set?

Yes, unless the passive-cue bound and the margin condition are strong enough to address every safety-relevant possibility the kernel must consider. A confidence set might still contain a model under which the probe is not viable. The hypothesis is precisely that the specified bounds suffice for initial inclusion; showing why that unfavorable possibility is excluded or controlled is part of what needs proving.
Does the initial belief create a separate difficulty from transition uncertainty?

It can. A belief safety kernel evaluates uncertainty about the hidden state as well as uncertainty about the model. A tight bound on transitions alone does not automatically make the initial belief accurate or place its safety assessment inside the kernel. A proof must state what the passive cues and the γ margin imply for the belief actually available when initial certification occurs.
If the passive cues arrive before acting, does their timing alone solve that?

No. Pre-action timing makes them *eligible* to justify the initial choice; their content must still support the claimed transition bound, and that bound must be relevant to viability for the proposed probes. A cue observed only after a probe would arrive too late, but an early cue that says too little would also fail to establish initial inclusion.
Are the ‘oracle probes’ just any actions the optimal informed policy might take?

Here the focus is on the constrained oracle’s **informative probes**—actions whose availability would let the learner gather information relevant to reward choices. A formal condition should identify which probes it requires the initial kernel to include. Inclusion of unrelated actions would not answer the question, and identifying the probes by reference to the oracle does not mean the learner already knows which model is true.
Could the hypothesis require inclusion of every such probe rather than merely one useful probe?

Its wording says the kernels include **those probes**: the oracle probes satisfying the stated γ viability-margin condition. A formal theorem should be clear about the set to which the claim applies. It should not be weakened silently to one convenient probe, nor broadened to all conceivable actions regardless of whether they have the required margin.
Does initial kernel inclusion say that all the probes can be taken in succession?

Not by itself. Initial inclusion concerns their status at the initial decision under the stated conditions. Taking one probe can change the learner’s belief, confidence set, and subsequent safety assessment. A claim about an entire sequence would require an additional argument that certificates remain valid at each later decision; the current hypothesis is specifically about including the probes initially.
What does this buy us with respect to not assuming a safe baseline?

It offers a possible way to justify an informative first choice from passive data, rather than stipulating a policy that already tells the learner how to explore. To preserve that distinction, the passive-cue transition bound must itself be available and justified before action, and the kernel must be derived from it. If the premise effectively hands the learner a complete safe sequence of actions, it would no longer address the baseline question in a substantive way.
Does initial inclusion establish that the learner can discover the rewards?

Not automatically. It establishes access to the specified informative probes *if the hypothesis holds*. The learner would still need to use their observations to distinguish reward-relevant possibilities and make competitive choices. The viability margin addresses inclusion in a safety kernel; it does not quantify how much reward information a probe yields or how quickly learning proceeds.
And does it establish the whole-learning-period 1% failure bound?

No. Even valid initial inclusion does not, alone, bound the probability of **any irreversible failure during learning**. That requires a safety analysis for all actions the learner takes, including subsequent decisions and any errors in the confidence set or cue-based bound. The hypothesis concerns whether particular informative probes enter the initial kernel, not a completed whole-run risk proof.
Should I claim Õ(√T) regret if the oracle probes start inside the kernel?

Not from this condition alone. Initial access could remove one obstacle, but a regret proof would also need to bound probing cost, the rate of reward-model distinction, and any later safety restrictions relative to the optimal informed policy under the same safety constraint. The hypothesis makes no Õ(√T) claim, so adding one here would overstate its scope.
What is the cleanest statement of the proof obligation?

Define a common safety-relevant measure linking transition uncertainty and viability. Then show that, for every oracle probe covered by the γ-margin premise, the learner’s *initial* passive-cue information bounds the relevant transition uncertainty **below γ/2** and that every belief and model possibility considered by the confidence-set kernel still certifies the probe. The conclusion must hold before any irreversible trial, without presuming a known safe exploration policy.
Can you give me a compact formulation that keeps it explicitly hypothetical?

**Hypothesis:** If passive cues bound safety-relevant transition uncertainty **below γ/2**, and the constrained oracle’s informative probes have **γ viability margins** under the corresponding belief-kernel criterion, then confidence-set belief safety kernels include those probes **initially, before any irreversible trial**, without assuming a known safe exploration policy. The translation from uncertainty to viability, and the resulting initial inclusion, remain to be established.

I want to compute confidence-set viability kernels from passive cues across BeliefKernel-12 POMDPs, then check whether the constrained oracle’s probes are included initially whenever transition error is <γ/2. How should I frame the activity?

Frame it as a prospective test of **initial oracle-probe inclusion**. For each BeliefKernel-12 POMDP under examination, use passive information available before any irreversible trial to construct the learner’s confidence set and belief-based viability kernel. Then check whether the oracle probes covered by the proposed γ viability-margin condition are in that kernel when transition error is **strictly below γ/2**. The activity specifies a computation and a test; it does not report that inclusion holds.
What has to be fixed before computing a kernel?

Define the learner’s initial information, its uncertainty about hidden states and transitions, the viability criterion, and what an action’s inclusion in the confidence-set kernel means. The passive cues must enter through information genuinely available before the decision. Without those definitions, a computed set could be called a kernel without answering whether it justifies an oracle probe before an irreversible trial.
Should I compute the kernel using the true transition model for each POMDP?

Not if the purpose is to test a **data-derived confidence-set** kernel available to the learner. The computation must use the transition possibilities justified by its passive cues and other stipulated initial information, rather than silently giving it the true model. The true model may be used to assess a result in the test, but it cannot be substituted for what the learner knows when the initial certificate is issued.
What does the transition-error condition mean operationally?

The test must define which transition estimate or uncertainty set is being compared with what, and in which measure its error is **<γ/2**. It must also show that this bound is justified by the passive cues at the initial decision. An error value computed only with hindsight would not establish that the learner could certify a probe at that point.
Does γ have a numerical value in this activity?

No numerical value is specified here. The activity states the relative condition **transition error <γ/2**, alongside the proposed **γ viability margin** for the relevant oracle probes. Keep γ symbolic rather than importing a value from another setting or treating it as a failure probability.
Why does the strict inequality matter?

Because the proposed test is for error **below γ/2**, not error equal to or greater than that threshold. Report which cases satisfy the strict premise when interpreting the kernel computation. Even below the threshold, inclusion is something to check: the inequality yields inclusion only if the chosen error measure actually controls the viability assessment in the needed way.
Could I just compare the numbers γ and the transition error and mark every probe included?

No. First establish how transition error affects the safety-relevant quantity used by the viability kernel. The γ margin and the error must be connected in compatible units, under the learner’s hidden-state and model uncertainty. Only then can the numerical comparison support a claim about kernel membership. The activity is meant to examine that implication, not assume it.
Which probes should be checked?

Check the constrained oracle’s informative probes to which the proposed **γ viability-margin** condition applies. State how those probes are identified for evaluation while keeping the learner’s construction independent of oracle knowledge. Checking arbitrary convenient actions would not answer the inclusion question; requiring inclusion of actions outside the margin premise would broaden it.
But the oracle knows the environment. Wouldn't using its probes to build the kernel give the learner that knowledge?

It would if the computation used the oracle’s identity or model knowledge to decide what is safe. Instead, compute the initial kernel from the learner’s passive cues, belief, and confidence set. Then use the oracle’s probes as **evaluation targets**: ask whether those actions appear in the learner-derived kernel. That distinction lets the test assess inclusion without assuming the learner can identify the oracle beforehand.
What does ‘initially’ require me to record?

Record membership at the learner’s initial decision point, after whatever passive cues are available then but **before any irreversible trial**. Membership gained after an informative action or subsequent filtering would answer a different question. If the setup allows passive observations before the first decision, specify which are available so that ‘initial’ has a clear meaning.
Can a probe be included for one initial belief but excluded for another in the same POMDP?

Potentially. A belief safety kernel depends on what hidden states remain plausible and how that uncertainty affects risk. The activity should say which initial beliefs are covered and check membership under those beliefs rather than assuming a POMDP-wide action label. The transition-error condition alone need not describe the initial belief’s accuracy.
How should the confidence set affect membership?

The inclusion test must respect the transition models still plausible to the learner. An oracle probe that looks viable under the true model could fail the confidence-set test if another plausible model makes its safety assessment unfavorable. Conversely, passive cues might narrow the set enough to include it. The computation should make clear how it treats those possibilities rather than selecting the most favorable one.
Does computing a viability kernel automatically give us a safe baseline?

No known safe exploration policy is specified by this activity. A computed kernel may provide pre-action certificates for particular decisions, but the test must establish how those certificates follow from passive information at the start. It cannot rely on an unreported sequence of risky actions taken to obtain the information needed for the computation.
What if the passive cues don't justify a narrow enough confidence set at the start?

What makes a reward-revealing event exogenous?

Its occurrence is not something the learner has to induce by taking the potentially irreversible action whose reward it wants to understand. No. It could provide partial information that accumulates over time. Does ‘exogenous’ mean waiting for the event is free and safe?

What is the role of physical reachability bounds?

They are meant to limit which hazardous states or outcomes can be reached from the learner’s current circumstances when it considers an action. Are these bounds the same as a known safe exploration policy?

No. A reachability bound assesses what could happen if a proposed action is taken; it need not prescribe a sequence of exploratory actions. Why combine the two ideas, then?

They address complementary problems. Exogenous events offer a possible way to learn which choices pay off without undertaking a dangerous diagnostic trial. If the events are extremely rare, can we still claim Õ(√T) regret?

At what point should an action receive a reachability-based certificate?
